title: Doors Opened: Women, Skaters of Color and Adaptive Skating
bigQuestion: Who was left out of skateboarding's early story, and how did the doors open wider?

story.title: Saturday Morning, All Ages
story.kicker: At an early all-ages session, a first-time grandmother and a wheelchair rider share the same concrete.
paragraphs: At nine on a Saturday morning, a city skatepark runs an all-ages beginner session before the afternoon crowd arrives. A volunteer sets out a box of loaner helmets and wrist guards on a folding table. A woman in her sixties picks out a helmet, buckles it, and pulls the strap snug under her chin. Her granddaughter, who is nine, shows her how to stand on a board sitting on the grass beside the concrete.

Across the park, a young man rolls his wheelchair to the edge of a small quarter pipe. He wears a helmet, elbow pads and gloves. He checks that his back wheels are on the coping, the metal edge at the top. Then he leans forward, tips in and rolls smoothly down the curved wall and across the flat bottom. Two kids on scooters clap.

In the middle of the park a teenage girl from the local skate club is teaching three younger girls how to push. She tells them to keep the front foot over the front bolts and push with the back foot. One girl wobbles, steps off and laughs. "Good," the teenager says. "Stepping off is how you stay safe. Again."

By ten-thirty the grandmother has rolled about three meters on the flat concrete, slowly, with her granddaughter walking beside her. When she steps off, the wheelchair rider gives her a fist bump. Fifty years ago, a scene like this one would have been very rare at a skatepark. Many people worked to make it ordinary.
story.think: What made this session welcoming to so many different people, and what would you add?

lessons.title: Patti McGee in 1965
lessons.mainIdea: Patti McGee won the women's title at the first national championships in 1965 and appeared on the cover of Life magazine that year.
reading: The first National Skateboard Championships were held in Anaheim, California, in 1965, and ABC's Wide World of Sports showed them on television. Patti McGee won the women's national title. At a time when many people thought of skating as something only boys did, a young woman was the champion on national TV.

That same year Life magazine, one of the most widely read magazines in the United States, put McGee on its cover. The photo showed her doing a *handstand* on a moving skateboard, barefoot, with her body straight above the board. A handstand on a rolling board takes strength, balance and practice. The cover carried skateboarding, and a woman skater, into millions of homes.

The first boom faded around 1965 and 1966, and many contests stopped. McGee's place in the story stayed, though. Later women skaters have named her as proof that girls were part of skateboarding from the start. Her story is a reminder that the record of who skated depends partly on who was photographed and written about, and that being seen can open a door for others.

lessons.title: Peggy Oki and the Zephyr Team
lessons.mainIdea: Peggy Oki was the only woman on the original Zephyr team, and she skated in the same low, surf-style way as her teammates.
reading: In the mid-1970s the Zephyr team came out of a surf shop in Santa Monica, California, near Venice. Its skaters, including Tony Alva, Jay Adams and Stacy Peralta, rode low to the ground, dragging a hand on the concrete the way a surfer touches a wave. Peggy Oki was the only woman on the original team, and she rode in that same style.

At the Del Mar Nationals in 1975, the Zephyr skaters surprised the crowd and the judges. Most competitors did upright freestyle routines. The Zephyr team crouched, carved hard and slid their boards in long, surf-like turns. Oki competed there with her teammates. Her skating showed that this new, aggressive style was not something only boys could do.

Oki later turned much of her energy to art, working as a painter. For later women who discovered the Zephyr story through magazines and the 2001 documentary Dogtown and Z-Boys, she became an important figure. Seeing one woman in a famous team photo showed many girls a place for themselves in the story.

a 1970s skate team from a Santa Monica surf shop, known for a low, surf-like style

The crowd has seen the first style many times. The second is new.

lessons.title: Women's Pro Careers Grow
lessons.mainIdea: Women skaters rode professionally from the 1970s on, but they had fewer contests, pro models and photos until skaters organized for change.
reading: In the late 1970s a few women, such as Laura Thornhill and Ellen O'Neal, rode for companies and appeared in magazines, mostly in *freestyle*: tricks done on flat ground, often in a planned routine. When many skateparks closed in the early 1980s, contests for everyone shrank, and women's events often disappeared first. For years many girls who skated rarely saw another woman at the park or in a magazine.

In the 1990s and 2000s more women turned pro in street and vert skating. Elissa Steamer, a street skater, became the first woman included in the video game Tony Hawk's Pro Skater in 1999. Millions of players saw her listed beside men. Women's events were added at more contests, but they often paid much less, had less TV time and were sometimes cut with little warning.

Women skaters answered by organizing. In the late 2000s a group of women pros pushed the X Games to pay women and men the same prize money, and the contest agreed. When skateboarding entered the Olympics, women and men had the same number of events, street and park for each. That *equal* structure was the result of decades of women showing up, skating and asking.

lessons.title: Teenage Women on the Olympic Podium
lessons.mainIdea: At Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024, young women from Japan, Brazil, Great Britain and Australia won Olympic medals, some at age 12 or 13.
reading: The IOC added skateboarding to the Olympic program in 2016, and it debuted at the Tokyo 2020 Games, held in 2021 because of the pandemic. In women's street, Momiji Nishiya of Japan won gold at age 13, and Rayssa Leal of Brazil, also 13, won silver. A *podium* is the stand where the top three finishers receive medals, and two of the three spots belonged to 13-year-olds.

In women's park at Tokyo, Sakura Yosozumi of Japan won gold, Kokona Hiraki of Japan won silver at age 12, and Sky Brown, 13, won bronze for Great Britain. At Paris 2024, Arisa Trew of Australia won women's park gold, and Coco Yoshizawa of Japan won women's street gold. Rayssa Leal earned a second Olympic medal in Paris, a bronze in street.

These results drew huge attention to girls' skating. News stories in several countries described more girls trying skating after the Games. The medalists also showed how young skaters can build very high skill when they start early and practice often, with coaching and support. Olympic results are official records kept by the IOC and World Skate, the sport's international federation.

lessons.title: Being Seen Changes Who Skates
lessons.mainIdea: When people see skaters who look like them in photos, videos and contests, more of them try skating, so coverage itself opens doors.
reading: For much of skating's history, magazines and videos mostly showed young men, often white and often from California. That did not mean only those people skated. Girls, older people, skaters of color and skaters in other countries were at parks and on streets, but they appeared in print much less. A *role model* is a person others look up to and learn from, and many skaters went years without seeing one who looked like them.

Coverage tends to feed itself. Companies sponsored the skaters who appeared in magazines, magazines photographed sponsored skaters, and young people copied what they saw. Breaking that loop took skaters, photographers and editors who chose to show more kinds of people. Online video helped too, because skaters could post their own clips without waiting to be chosen.

In media, *representation* means who is shown and how. Today it is common to see women, adaptive riders and skaters from many countries in contests, videos and ads. Skate groups often say that seeing someone like you on a board makes the first visit to a park feel possible. For a beginner, a single friendly face at the park can do the same thing.

who is shown in photos, videos and media, and how they are shown

sections.title: Skaters of Color and the World

lessons.title: Ray Barbee and Smooth Street Style
lessons.mainIdea: Ray Barbee, a Black skater on the Bones Brigade in the late 1980s, became known for a smooth, flowing flat-ground street style.
reading: Ray Barbee grew up skating in San Jose, California, and joined Powell Peralta's Bones Brigade in the late 1980s. He was one of the few Black skaters on a famous team at a time when most skate magazines showed few skaters of color. His part in the 1989 Powell Peralta video Ban This made many viewers notice how relaxed and smooth street skating could look.

Barbee's style used flat ground and small objects rather than big ramps. He linked tricks such as no-complies, manuals and quick turns into one flowing line. A *line* is a series of tricks done one after another in a single run, without stopping. Watching a good line is a little like watching a dancer move across a stage.

Barbee is also a musician who plays guitar, and he later released his own records. Many skaters point to him as an example that style, meaning how a trick looks and feels, matters as much as difficulty. He showed young Black skaters someone like them in the most famous skate videos of the time, and he has stayed part of the skate community for decades.

words.d: a Black skater from San Jose on the late-1980s Bones Brigade, known for smooth street style
a series of tricks done one after another in a single run, without stopping
how a skater's tricks look and feel, apart from how hard they are

She keeps pushing without stopping, arms loose, the whole run looking easy.

lessons.title: Stevie Williams and Nyjah Huston
lessons.mainIdea: Stevie Williams rose from Philadelphia's Love Park to start his own company, and Nyjah Huston became one of the most successful contest skaters ever.
reading: Stevie Williams grew up in Philadelphia and became known in the 1990s skating Love Park, a downtown plaza with granite ledges and steps that drew skaters from around the world. He turned pro young and, in the early 2000s, started his own skateboard company, DGK. Owning a company meant he could sponsor and promote other skaters, many from city neighborhoods like his own, instead of waiting for others to choose them.

Love Park also shows how cities and skaters have argued over public space. Philadelphia restricted skating there in the early 2000s, and many skaters and fans pushed back. The fight showed how much a spot can matter to a community. Questions about where skating is allowed are still debated in many cities.

Nyjah Huston, born in 1994, became one of the most successful contest skaters in history. He has won many titles in Street League Skateboarding, a street contest series, and many X Games medals. He competed for the United States at Tokyo 2020 and won bronze in men's street at Paris 2024. Huston and Williams, in different ways, showed young skaters of color a clear path to the top of the sport.

lessons.title: Skating in Brazil and Japan
lessons.mainIdea: Brazil and Japan built strong skate scenes that produced Olympic champions, showing that skateboarding's center is no longer only California.
reading: Skateboarding spread far beyond the United States. Brazil has one of the largest skate communities in the world, with busy public parks and many skaters in street, park and vert. Bob Burnquist, who grew up in Brazil, became a famous vert skater at the X Games. At the Olympics, Rayssa Leal won a medal for Brazil in women's street at both Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024.

Japan's results were just as striking. At Tokyo 2020, Yuto Horigome won the first Olympic gold in men's street, in the city where he grew up. Momiji Nishiya won women's street gold and Sakura Yosozumi won women's park gold. At Paris 2024, Horigome won men's street again and Coco Yoshizawa won women's street gold.

Strong scenes like these usually grow from many small things: public parks, local shops, coaches, friends who skate together and families who support practice. Skaters in Australia, South Africa, Europe and many other places have their own histories too. The *global* spread of skating means a beginner today can find a crew, a video or a role model from almost anywhere.

lessons.title: WCMX and Aaron Fotheringham
lessons.mainIdea: WCMX is riding a skatepark in a wheelchair, and Aaron Fotheringham showed what is possible when he landed the first wheelchair backflip in the mid-2000s.
reading: *WCMX*, short for wheelchair motocross, means riding a skatepark's ramps, bowls and ledges in a wheelchair. Riders use strong, specially built chairs, often with extra wheels or suspension, and they wear helmets and pads like any skater. The same ideas apply as on a board: lean into a ramp, keep your weight centered, and learn to fall safely before trying bigger moves.

Aaron Fotheringham, from Las Vegas, was born with spina bifida and has used a wheelchair for most of his life. As a boy he rode at a skatepark with his brother, who rode a BMX bike. In the mid-2000s he landed the first wheelchair backflip, rolling up a ramp and turning a full circle backward in the air before landing. Clips of it spread widely online, and he later performed in live action-sports shows around the world.

Adaptive skating is a wider family. It includes wheelchair riders, skaters with prosthetic legs, skaters who are blind or have low vision, and people who ride sitting or kneeling on a board. The word *adaptive* means changing the equipment or the way a skill is done so it fits a person's body. Many parks now hold adaptive sessions, and riders teach each other new ways to drop in, turn and fall.

If she leans back, the chair tips backward, so the coach reminds her: chest forward, eyes ahead.

lessons.title: Groups That Open the Gate
lessons.mainIdea: Groups such as Skateistan and The Skatepark Project, plus local girls' and adaptive sessions, work on purpose to bring new people into skating.
reading: Skateistan began in Kabul, Afghanistan, in 2007, founded by Oliver Percovich, an Australian skater. It used skateboarding to bring children into a safe place and into classes, and it made a special effort to welcome girls. It later opened programs in other countries, including Cambodia and South Africa. Its work showed that a skateboard can be a doorway to school and community.

In the United States, the Tony Hawk Foundation began in 2002 to help communities build public skateparks, especially in places with few resources. It was renamed The Skatepark Project in 2020. Local groups add to this work by running *girls' sessions*, adaptive sessions, older-adult sessions and free loaner gear, often at quiet hours when the park is less crowded.

These groups use a few simple moves that any park can copy. They lend helmets and pads so cost is not a barrier. They set times when beginners will not feel rushed. They train volunteers to teach, starting on grass or flat ground. Most of all, they make sure a new person is greeted by name. A *barrier* is anything that keeps someone from starting, such as cost, fear, distance or not seeing anyone like you.

lessons.title: A Place Where Many Belong
lessons.mainIdea: Skateparks work best for everyone when riders share space with simple habits: take turns, watch your line and welcome newcomers.
reading: A busy skatepark has no referee, so riders follow unwritten rules called *park etiquette*. Wait at the edge and take turns dropping in. Look before you roll so you do not cut across someone's path. Do not sit on obstacles or stand in landing zones. If you fall, move off quickly. These habits keep a park safe for a nine-year-old, a sixty-year-old and a wheelchair rider at the same time.

Belonging also comes from small social habits. Experienced skaters often cheer when someone lands a first trick, even a very small one, and that cheer means a lot to a beginner. Tapping a board on the ground is a common way to applaud. Older skaters and adults starting late are part of this too; many parks now see people in their forties, fifties and older learning for the first time or coming back.

Skating has always mixed many kinds of people, even when photos did not show it. The doors opened by Patti McGee, Peggy Oki, Ray Barbee, Elissa Steamer, Aaron Fotheringham, the teenage Olympic medalists and countless local volunteers make today's parks more open than ever. A *community* is a group of people who share a place or an interest and look out for each other. Every rider can help build one.
